objectives.reply: I made the first cut myself, and I told it first. It did not answer. That was the worst of it. I am carving a bench from the first ring, for the Chapel, with one name on it: the Oak. The town will be warm for twenty winters and cold for a hundred years of memory. Take this heartwood. Do not burn it. Make something that can be sat on.

quests.outro: A bench of heartwood sits before the Chapel of Chorrol, with a single word carved on it. The town is warm, and does not speak of the Oak above a whisper.

quests.title: The Walk to the Legion
quests.pitch: Harbourmaster Teodor Arenius walked to the Legion himself. Marga the Net-Mender has news.
quests.desc: Harbourmaster Teodor Arenius walked to the Legion himself. Marga the Net-Mender has news.

objectives.text: Hear from Marga what became of the Harbourmaster
objectives.topic: Teodor confessed. What happened to him?
objectives.reply: He walked up the quay at noon with the tally book under his arm, and gave it to the Legion captain himself. They kept him in the cells for a month and let him out on a bond. He is the Keeper's assistant now, trimming wicks. I do not forgive him. I do not need to. He climbs the stair every dusk, and the lamp has not gone dim since. Take this. It is my best net-needle.

quests.outro: Teodor Arenius trims the wicks of the Anvil lighthouse under the Keeper's eye. Nobody in the harbour has forgiven him, and nobody sleeps badly.

quests.title: A Debt in Brass
quests.pitch: You kept the wreckers' book from the Legion. Harbourmaster Teodor Arenius says he owes you.
quests.desc: You kept the wreckers' book from the Legion. Harbourmaster Teodor Arenius says he owes you.

objectives.text: Collect on the Harbourmaster's debt
objectives.topic: You said you owed me a debt.
objectives.reply: I do. A man like me does not forget. Here is a harbour pass: it opens every gate on the quay, at any hour, and no tally will record it. I wish I could give you more. I wish I could give my brother what he is owed. Instead I give you a key. Use it well. And if you ever see a lamp go dim in Anvil, you will know whose fault it is.

quests.outro: The Harbourmaster of Anvil has paid his debt in a pass and a promise. The beacon burns, and the tally book is ash, and nobody has asked.

quests.title: Read from the Steps
quests.pitch: Captain Pellia Vorn read the Founders' Charter from the temple steps. She has news.
quests.desc: Captain Pellia Vorn read the Founders' Charter from the temple steps. She has news.

objectives.text: Hear how Bravil took the reading of the charter
objectives.topic: You read the charter. How did the city take it?
objectives.reply: Loudly. Mother Nettle wept. Tomas Fenn tied a lucky knot in my sleeve and refused to take it off. The Count's clerk left on the morning boat. The tithe is paid to the poor now, from a box that the Lady holds in her hand, and every coin is counted twice. Ulrich was gone before the reading ended. I found a slate on my desk: THANK YOU. He will not be back.

quests.outro: The tithe of Bravil is paid to the poor of the town from the hand of the Lucky Old Lady. Ulrich the Quiet is somewhere else, and has, one hopes, found a place to speak.

quests.title: The Quiet Charter
quests.pitch: The charter went back under the Lady. Mother Nettle suspects what you did, and has a word.
quests.desc: The charter went back under the Lady. Mother Nettle suspects what you did, and has a word.

objectives.text: Hear what Mother Nettle makes of the buried charter
objectives.topic: The charter is buried. You suspect it?
objectives.reply: Suspect? Child, I have been at the foot of that stair for sixty winters. I know when the Lady has been disturbed. You put the thing back, and somebody smarter than I put a coin in her hand last night, and it was not a copper. Say nothing. I shall say nothing. It is the oldest way to keep a promise, and the quietest, and the surest. Take this. It is only an eel, but it is a very good eel.

quests.outro: The charter lies beneath the Lady, undisturbed. Someone leaves a gold coin in her hand each dawn, and Mother Nettle says it is only the tide.
